title: Making it better: memper-
goal: Understand and use the memper- verbs that turn a quality into an action (longer, wider, better, more) and the big everyday ones like memperhatikan and mempelajari, in their active, passive and object-focus forms.
bekal: say what needs fixing, extending or improving: *memperbaiki, memperpanjang, memperluas*
use the key abstract memper- verbs: *memperhatikan, mempelajari, mempertimbangkan*
switch to *diper-* and object-focus: *perlu diperbaiki, kami perbanyak*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Keliling rumah Bu Ratna
dialogs.intro: A week after the first meeting. Bu Ratna shows Sarah round her house, one of eight in Sumberwangi that the women's group want to turn into homestays.

notes: **Monggo** is Javanese for "please, go ahead, after you", and in Central Java it is part of everyday Indonesian: *monggo masuk*, *monggo diminum* (please, have your drink). The Indonesian equivalent is *silakan*. You will hear *monggo* from Bu Ratna far more often than *silakan*.

**Menjadikan** — "to make into, turn into" — from *jadi*. *Kamar yang mau kami jadikan homestay* is object-focus: "the room that we want to make into a homestay". It is a very useful verb: *Dia menjadikan rumahnya warung* (she turned her house into a food stall).

**Nanti suami saya yang memperbaiki.** The *yang* here points at who does it: "it's my husband who'll fix it". Indonesian uses this *X yang* + verb pattern to put a person in focus, and Unit 17 comes back to it.

**Kloset jongkok and kloset duduk.** The squat toilet and the sitting toilet. A village bathroom also has a *bak mandi* (water tank), a *gayung* (dipper) and often an *ember* (bucket). For guests the bathroom question is real, and Sarah's answer is the honest one: clean matters more than modern.

**Sebaiknya** means "it would be best to, we'd better". It is the polite way to recommend something without giving an order: *Sebaiknya Bapak istirahat dulu* (you should rest first, sir). Much gentler than *harus*.

**Siap!** literally "ready", has become the all-purpose "yes, will do, got it", borrowed from military usage. Staff say it to bosses, friends say it to friends. With elders, *siap, Bu* is fine; in writing prefer *baik*.

grammars.title: memper- + adjective: making something more so
body: Put *memper-* in front of an adjective and you get a verb meaning "to make (something) more X". Some add *-i*. The root is almost always an adjective of size, quantity or quality.
after: You will meet these everywhere official: *memperpanjang KITAS* (extend your stay permit), *memperbarui data* (update your details), *jalan sedang diperbaiki* (road under repair).

💬 In speech, many of these give way to shorter forms: *benerin* (fix), *gedein* (make bigger), *panjangin* (lengthen). Bu Ratna's village register sits between the two, which is why she says *diperbaiki* but also *sama* instead of *dan*.

grammars.title: The big abstract ones: memper-…-kan and memper-…-i
body: A second group of memper- verbs has drifted from its roots and simply has to be learnt as vocabulary. These are among the most frequent verbs in written Indonesian.
after: ⚠️ *Mempelajari* loses the *r*: *per- + ajar* gives *pel-ajar*, as in *pelajar* (pupil) and *pelajaran* (lesson). Never *memperlajari*.

*Belajar* vs *mempelajari*: *belajar bahasa Jawa* is "learning Javanese" in general; *mempelajari bahasa Jawa* is studying it carefully, as an object. Only the second takes a direct object comfortably in formal writing.

dialogs.title: Second dialogue — Rencana konten Yoga
dialogs.intro: A few days later at Sarah's office in Yogyakarta. Yoga, the UGM intern, has a plan for the village's social media. Mas Bayu is listening in.

lines.text: Oke, boleh diganti. Tapi rencananya kita pelajari dulu bareng Pak Harun, ya.

notes: **Aku with his boss.** Yoga uses *aku* with Sarah, where an older Indonesian employee would say *saya*. Among young urban Indonesians *aku* has become the neutral "I" with anyone who is not clearly senior or formal. Sarah, older and the coordinator, lets it go; Pak Harun would notice.

**Yog!** Indonesians shorten names when calling someone: *Yog* for Yoga, *Sar* for Sarah, *Dim* for Dimas. It is friendly and casual, and only used when addressing the person directly, never when talking about them.

**Taunya cuma Borobudur** — "all they know is Borobudur". *Taunya* is spoken *tahunya* (their knowing), and *cuma* is spoken *hanya* (only). The *-nya* turns the verb into a noun, a job you saw it do in A2 Unit 17.

**Unggah** is the official Indonesian for "upload" (and *unduh* for "download"). Yoga actually says *unggah* here because he is pitching to his supervisor; in a chat with friends he would type *upload* or *up*. Both are understood everywhere.

**Jangan asal rekam.** *Asal* + verb means "to do something carelessly, without thinking": *asal ngomong* (talk without thinking), *asal pilih* (choose at random). Different from the *asal* in Unit 1's "as long as"; context decides.

**Emang, bakal, gaul.** Three pieces of young spoken Indonesian: *emang* = *memang* (indeed; "why, ...?" at the start of a question), *bakal* = *akan* (will), and *gaul* = sociable, trendy, cool. *Kurang gaul* (not cool enough) is gentle teasing; its cousin *kudet*, from *kurang update*, means "behind the times".

grammars.title: memper- or me-…-kan? Close pairs
body: Some roots take both *memper-* and *me-…-kan*, and the meanings drift apart. Learn them as pairs; the difference is real and Indonesians notice it.

head: me-…-kan
Meaning
memper-
Meaning
rows: to play a song for others

after: Rule of thumb: the *memper-* form is more formal, more deliberate, and more likely to be about an institution or a project. The *me-…-kan* form is more physical and everyday.

In object-focus and in imperatives the prefix simply drops, leaving *per-*: *Perhatikan!* (Pay attention!), *kita pelajari*, *kami perbanyak*. Health posters say *Perbanyak minum air putih* (drink more water).

sections.title: The memper- verbs on signs and forms

blocks.text: Once you know the prefix, you will start seeing it on every notice board. These are real phrases you will meet in Indonesia; each one uses a memper- verb in its passive or imperative form.
Notice *memperbanyak* in the fifth line: "to multiply" becomes "to copy, reproduce". The front page of almost every Indonesian book carries that warning.
Fixing up a village house needs a small, concrete vocabulary. Bu Ratna's group used every one of these words in their first week.

items: *Bocor* is "leaking" for roofs, tyres and pipes; in slang it also means leaking a secret.
*Ulang* after a verb means "again, re-": *dicat ulang* (repainted), *dicek ulang* (rechecked).
*Tukang* combines with a trade: *tukang kayu* (carpenter), *tukang listrik* (electrician), *tukang ledeng* (plumber).
